text.tagline: Me then, me now, what’s better, and how?
text.story:
The drawer sticks.

Rory pushes harder.

The drawing disappears.

Aunt Tess sits beside the table. “That looked like a drawing you didn't want to see.” Rory keeps hold of the drawer handle, even though it is already shut.

“My best friend won. I wanted to win.” Their voice drops. “I am jealous, and now I feel horrible for not being happy for my friend.”

“You care about your friend, and you wanted that prize,” Aunt Tess says. “You don't have to put on a cheerful face for me.”

“Can both things be true?” Rory asks. “It feels like a contradiction. Like one feeling should cancel the other.” Aunt Tess shakes her head. “Both can be here.”

Rory lets go of the handle. “Everything I made feels worse now.” Aunt Tess glances at the drawer. “Could we look at your work beside your own earlier work, instead?”

“Tell me how,” Rory says. “Without the cheering section.”

“Pick one thing you're working on. Piano, free throws, long division, anything. Think back a month, or a year. What could you do then? Say it. Now what can you do today? Say it. Now one more: what helped you get from then to now? A new way of practicing? Someone who showed you? That's your progress. Nobody else's score is in this picture.”

Rory opens the drawer and finds an older painting underneath today's drawing. They place the older sheet on the left and today's work on the right. “These are both mine.”

The old painting has a leaf surrounded by a watery blur. The new drawing has painted leaves with narrow spaces between them. Rory studies those spaces without speaking.

They point left. “Then, the colours ran together.” They point right. “Now I can keep these edges separate.” Their finger stops beside one leaf. “Mostly. This one's escaping.”

“What helped that change?” Aunt Tess asks. Rory looks closer. “I started letting one bit dry before painting beside it. Less water on the brush, too.”

Rory pinches their soft eraser into a pointing finger. It droops across both sheets. “Excellent. My assistant has selected everything.” Aunt Tess laughs.

“The edges are evidence,” Rory says. “Something I can actually point to. Not just you saying it's nice because you live with me.”

Aunt Tess lowers her voice. “Comparing with their past selves helped children from eight to sixteen feel proud. That was one short test, so we don't know how long it lasts.”

“I like those leaves,” Rory admits. Then their mouth tightens. “I still wish I'd won.” They wait, as if that might mean the whole comparison has failed.

“You noticed a change and what helped it,” Aunt Tess says. “You don't have to trade your disappointment for that.” She leaves both sheets where Rory put them.

Rory looks from left to right again. They can see the difference. They can also picture the prize beside their friend's work, and that still stings.

“I care about my friend. And I'm jealous,” they say. “I don't have a cheerful version.” Aunt Tess stays beside them. “I'm listening to this version.”

Rory nudges the drooping eraser away from the wet paint. They leave both pictures on the table. “They can both stay.”

recordAtStart.familyContext: Rory uses they/them pronouns and lives with Aunt Tess. Please do not turn this into a competition with their friend or promise Rory the next prize.

tonight: Rory is 12 and lives with me, Aunt Tess. Their best friend won the school art prize and Rory did not. Rory said, "I am jealous, and now I feel horrible for not being happy for my friend." They shoved their drawing into a drawer. I want to make room for both feelings without forcing them to cheer up.
